title: Connectivity diagnosis without jargon
quick: Start by separating availability, affordability, reliability, devices, skills, accessibility and useful-service needs. A faster advertised plan does not solve every barrier.
steps: Check whether fixed or mobile service is actually available at the location.
Record price, advertised speed and several measured speed/latency observations.
List devices and critical uses: school, work, telehealth, business and emergency communications.
Identify the bottleneck before selecting an intervention.
advanced: Treat effective access as a chain: infrastructure → service offer → affordability → device → skills/accessibility → reliable use → beneficial service. One failed link can dominate the outcome.
expert: For community analysis, keep provider-reported availability, measured performance, subscription/adoption and affordability in separate fields. Preserve date, geography, methodology and source provenance.
pitfalls: Do not substitute one speed test for an availability finding.
Do not treat advertised speed as delivered reliability.
handoffs: Navigator → ISP/FCC/BDO pathway for availability discrepancies
verification: Repeat tests under documented conditions; record plan price, technology, date, device and Wi‑Fi path.

title: Decentralized multiplayer with Trystero + WebRTC
quick: Hosted/online users start in the shared public Texas commons. Trystero helps browsers discover one another; shared room records then travel browser-to-browser over WebRTC rather than through an application data server. Custom rooms remain available.
steps: Start in the default public room and treat display names, roles and peer IDs as unverified coordination metadata.
For non-public work, choose a hard-to-guess custom room ID; optionally add a shared password.
Choose a discovery strategy (Nostr is the default; MQTT, BitTorrent and IPFS are alternatives).
Confirm peer presence, then share only records appropriate for that room. Each browser keeps its own IndexedDB copy.
If direct WebRTC cannot traverse a restrictive network, configure an explicit TURN fallback and document that relay dependency.
advanced: Trystero abstracts WebRTC signaling while its makeAction API carries application events, serialization, chunking and peer targeting. v5 tags every synchronized record with its collaboration room and sends only active-room records in join snapshots. Discovery media exchange session information; application payloads use the resulting WebRTC connection.
expert: This suite pins the browser integration to Trystero 0.25.3 semantics and a v5-specific app ID. It uses action objects (send/onMessage) from the 0.25 API. The public room is passwordless by design, custom rooms can use a shared password, and Internal/Sensitive records are retained locally rather than broadcast from the public commons. The mesh remains room-scoped because browsers have finite peer-connection capacity.
pitfalls: Peer IDs, display names, roles and organization labels are not verified identities.
A room password improves session-description secrecy but is not institutional identity/access management.
Do not assume that local IndexedDB records from another room should be shared; v5 room-scopes snapshots to prevent this.
TURN may relay encrypted WebRTC traffic when direct paths fail; disclose and govern the relay.
handoffs: Institution IT → TURN/network-policy and approved-room design
Project lead → participants for room purpose/password exchange
Privacy/evidence lead → record classification and retention rules
verification: Open two hosted browsers/devices, confirm both enter the public room, create a public task and decision, then verify room-scoped snapshot convergence. Repeat with a custom room and confirm records from the public room are not included.

title: Reading Texas broadband project status correctly
quick: Do not treat an announcement or award as an active connection. Track the lifecycle separately: selected/awarded → engineering/permitting → construction → activation → adoption.
steps: Open the dated BDO/NTIA source.
Record geography and locations/premises covered.
Record technology and expected performance.
Record current project stage and verification date.
Only call a location operational when activation is actually verified.
advanced: Program totals can describe selected applicants or eligible locations without proving every premise is built or subscribing. Maintain status at project/location granularity when possible.
expert: Join administrative award data to coverage/location data only with compatible identifiers and vintage. Preserve uncertainty when award boundaries or Broadband Serviceable Location counts change.
pitfalls: Do not call an award “built.”
Do not aggregate location counts across incompatible vintages without labels.
handoffs: Institution → project lead for anchor-institution requirements
Community → evidence team for activation verification
verification: Verify project status against the newest BDO map/files and record retrieval date plus lifecycle state.

title: Broadband map challenge workflow
quick: If an official map says service is available but it is not actually orderable, document the discrepancy and use the official challenge process.
steps: Capture the map claim and date.
Try the provider's normal ordering process and retain evidence.
Record address/location evidence without publishing sensitive household details.
Submit through the current official FCC/BDO process.
Track the challenge outcome separately from your original observation.
advanced: An availability challenge disputes a service claim; it is not the same as a speed-test complaint. Performance evidence can support local investigation but should not be mislabeled as verified availability data.
expert: For aggregate community analysis, classify observations by evidence type, deduplicate locations, and avoid converting voluntary reports into population prevalence estimates without a defensible sampling method.
pitfalls: Do not publish household addresses in an open room.
Do not infer statewide prevalence from voluntary complaints.
verification: Retain screenshots/order evidence privately; record challenge ID/outcome without exposing sensitive location data publicly.

title: Cross-domain project design
audience: Schools, clinics, libraries, counties, utilities, workforce teams
quick: A connectivity project is stronger when each affected discipline owns a concrete dependency and outcome instead of merely being named as a partner.
steps: Define the connectivity barrier and geography.
Add each affected domain: education, health, workforce, emergency, energy, water, mobility, agriculture, libraries or public services.
Assign an owner for each dependency.
Choose shared metrics and verification dates.
Record decisions, evidence and unresolved assumptions in the room.
advanced: Use dependency mapping: connectivity inputs enable service capabilities, but service outcomes also depend on staffing, devices, accessibility, workflow, policy, power resilience and user adoption.
expert: Model cross-domain work as a typed dependency graph. Prevent double counting by separating infrastructure outputs, service capabilities, utilization and downstream outcomes.
pitfalls: Avoid “partner theater”: every partner should own a dependency/output.
Do not double-count downstream benefits as direct infrastructure outputs.
verification: Every project should have owners, dependencies, metrics, evidence class, verification date and handoff status.

title: Telehealth connectivity readiness
quick: A video visit needs more than download speed: reliable upload, low disruption, a usable camera/microphone, privacy, accessibility and support matter.
steps: Test connection quality at the place the visit will occur.
Check camera, microphone and browser/app compatibility.
Choose a private, accessible location.
Create a backup phone/contact plan.
For community rooms, define cleaning, privacy and support procedures.
advanced: Latency, jitter and packet loss can harm interactive sessions even when throughput looks adequate. Test at representative times and on the actual Wi-Fi/device path.
expert: Do not infer clinical quality from connectivity alone. Keep telecommunications readiness separate from clinical appropriateness, consent, privacy and provider workflow requirements.
pitfalls: Connectivity readiness is not clinical suitability.
Public/community telehealth rooms need privacy and accessibility procedures.
verification: Test on the actual device/location/time; document latency/jitter/packet loss where available and confirm backup contact procedure.

title: Emergency communications resilience
quick: Plan for broadband, cellular and power failures as separate events that can happen together.
steps: List critical communications functions.
Identify primary, alternate and contingency channels.
Estimate router/modem/device backup runtime.
Keep offline copies of essential procedures and contacts.
Exercise the plan and record what failed.
advanced: Redundancy only helps when failure modes are sufficiently independent. Two services sharing the same upstream fiber or power dependency may fail together.
expert: Use fault-tree or dependency analysis for critical sites: access circuit, middle mile, DNS, power, local LAN/Wi-Fi, device fleet, identity systems and staffing.
pitfalls: Redundant services may share the same fiber, tower or power dependency.
Do not rely on cloud-only procedures during an outage.
verification: Exercise primary/alternate/contingency communications and record restoration times and common-mode failures.

title: Local WebLLM planning assistant
quick: WebLLM can run a compatible language model locally in a supported browser. It is optional; the OS still provides deterministic tools when local AI is unavailable.
steps: Check WebGPU/browser capability.
Load the model catalog only when online.
Choose a model sized for device memory.
Keep source notes in the prompt and verify generated claims.
Unload the model when finished on memory-constrained devices.
advanced: Model weights can be large and may be cached by the WebLLM runtime. Local inference improves data locality but does not make model output automatically factual.
expert: Treat generated plans as hypotheses/work products. Retain source IDs and separate sourced facts, assumptions, calculations and proposed actions before institutional use.
pitfalls: Local inference does not make generated claims true.
Model downloads may be large and require network access before offline reuse.
Do not paste secrets or protected personal data into prompts.
handoffs: Research lead → AI user with verified source packet
verification: Require source IDs for factual claims and distinguish sourced facts, calculations, assumptions and generated proposals.

title: PWA and offline mode
quick: When hosted over HTTPS, the service worker caches the application shell and core reference data. Your project records live in IndexedDB. Live websites and peer discovery still require network connectivity.
steps: Host the folder over HTTPS.
Open once online so the service worker can install.
Install the PWA if the browser offers it.
Export periodic JSON backups.
Check freshness labels after working offline.
advanced: The service worker uses a versioned cache for same-origin assets. Third-party Trystero/WebLLM modules are network capabilities and are not falsely presented as guaranteed offline dependencies.
expert: For controlled deployments, vendor audited dependency builds under the same origin and update CSP/SRI/hash manifests as part of a reproducible release process.
pitfalls: Service workers require HTTP(S), not file://.
Cached reference data can become stale.
Third-party model/discovery networks are not guaranteed offline.
verification: After install, disconnect network and confirm shell/reference pages and IndexedDB records still open; label unavailable live features.

title: Evidence and provenance for public planning
quick: Every important number should answer: who published it, when, for what geography, using what dataset or method, and with what limitation?
steps: Prefer official measured/administrative data when available.
Store publication and retrieval dates.
Record geography and definitions.
Keep modeled scenarios visibly separate from observations.
Re-verify time-sensitive programs before acting.
advanced: A reliable evidence registry is as important as the number itself because definitions and program status change over time.
expert: Use stable source identifiers, schema versioning, licensing metadata and reproducible transforms when deriving indicators. Hashes establish byte integrity, not authorship.
